t: Split Message Based on Limit — Editorial
o: We must cut `message` into `b` pieces so that piece `a` carries the next chunk of characters plus the suffix `<a/b>`, every non-last piece has length exactly `limit`, and the last piece has length at most `limit`. The catch: `b` appears inside every suffix, so we cannot know the suffix sizes until we fix `b`. For a fixed `b`, piece `a` can carry at most `limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b)` message characters, so the split works iff the total capacity over `a = 1..b` is at least `len(message)` (the leftover simply sits in the last piece). In example 1 (`limit = 9`), trying `b = 14`: parts 1–9 hold 4 chars each (suffix `<a/14>` has length 5), parts 10–14 hold 3 chars each, giving capacity 9·4 + 5·3 = 51 ≥ 36, and smaller `b` values fail — hence 14 parts. Constraints are tiny (`n ≤ 10⁴`), so enumerating candidate values of `b` from small to large and taking the first feasible one is exactly right.
k: For a fixed total count b, the maximum characters piece a can hold is limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b); feasibility is just whether these capacities sum to at least len(message).
Trying b = 1, 2, 3, ... and stopping at the first feasible value automatically minimizes the number of parts.
If limit - 3 - 2·digits(b) ≤ 0 no character fits, so such b is hopeless; since capacity grows once it becomes positive, b never needs to exceed len(message).

a.i: For each candidate total count b starting from 1, recompute the full capacity by looping over all indices a = 1..b and summing `limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b)`. The first b whose capacity reaches `len(message)` is optimal because we scan in increasing order. This is simple and directly mirrors the feasibility argument; with n ≤ 10⁴ it easily passes even though the check is O(b) per candidate.
s: For each b, compute capacity = Σ_{a=1..b} max(0, limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b)); skip b immediately if even the largest piece has no room.
If capacity ≥ n, stop: this b is minimal.
Rebuild the answer: walk through message taking chunks of size limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b) and append the suffix <a/b>; the final remainder forms the last piece.
If b exceeds n without success, return an empty array.
a.t: O(n · √n)-ish worst case — for each candidate b we spend O(b) checking capacity, and b is bounded by n; trivially fast for n ≤ 10⁴.

a.i: Instead of recomputing the capacity from scratch for every candidate b, maintain it incrementally: when moving from b-1 to b, all previous pieces' capacities shrink only if digits(b) changed, and we add the new piece's capacity. Concretely, keep a running sum and subtract `digits(newB) - digits(oldB)` per existing piece when the digit count of b increases. Each candidate is now checked in O(1) amortized time, giving overall O(n) work plus output construction.
s: Initialize b = 1, running capacity cap = limit - 3 - 1 - 1 (for index 1 and total 1).

While cap < n: set b ← b + 1; if digits(b) > digits(b-1), subtract (digits(b) - digits(b-1)) · (b - 1) from cap; then add limit - 3 - digits(b) - digits(b) for the new piece; if that term is ≤ 0 or b > n, return [].
Once cap ≥ n, slice message into b chunks of size limit - 3 - digits(a) - digits(b) and attach suffixes.
The first feasible b found is minimal since we scan upward.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def splitMessage(self, message: str, limit: int) -> List[str]:
        n = len(message)
        b, cap = 1, limit - 5
        while cap < n and b <= n:
            nb = b + 1
            d_old, d_new = len(str(b)), len(str(nb))
            cap -= (d_new - d_old) * b
            cap += limit - 3 - 2 * d_new
            b = nb
        if cap < n:
            return []
        db = len(str(b))
        res, i = [], 0
        for a in range(1, b + 1):
            sz = limit - 3 - len(str(a)) - db
            res.append(message[i:i + sz] + "<" + str(a) + "/" + str(b) + ">")
            i += sz
        return res

a.t: O(n) — the capacity loop advances b one step at a time with O(1) amortized updates, bounded by b ≤ n, plus O(n) to build the answer.

w: In an interview, present the fixed-b capacity formula first — it collapses the whole problem into 'find the smallest b whose total capacity covers len(message)'. Then mention the incremental trick as the optimization. Common pitfalls: forgetting the suffix adds 3 characters for '<', '/', '>' plus the digits of both a and b; assuming all suffixes have equal length (they don't — digits(a) varies); off-by-one on the last piece (it may be shorter than limit, which is allowed); and mishandling tiny limits (e.g., limit ≤ 4 is always impossible since even '<1/1>' has length 5). Edge cases worth testing: message shorter than a single part, limit exactly equal to suffix size plus one character, and limits where increasing b eventually makes suffixes too large. A likely follow-up: can you binary-search b instead of scanning linearly? Yes — capacity is monotone in b within blocks of constant digits(b), though the piecewise jumps make careful handling necessary; linear scan is simpler and already optimal here.
